My long term thoughts on the RX 6900XT as an owner of this card:
I've been having near constant problems with windows overwriting my video driver with their drivers for the AMD cards which basically make AMD Radeon Software Unusable. I've had to make many sacrifices and tricks with AMD software just to get some games playable. Others just refuse to start and otherwise crash randomly. Most recently I have started my first play-through for Red Dead Redemption 2 on PC and have had lots of trouble keeping it running on my 6900XT. The main problem is "Unknown Error: Code FFFFF" every 2 hours which causes the game to crash. I've verified game file integrity, I've changed the drivers and rolled them back to AMD's latest recommended by AMD software, I've changed the virtual RAM allocation for 4-8GB per disk on my system,  I've even completely clean installed all AMD drivers. No matter what I do, it has done this three times. I run an AMD CPU too  (The 5950X) and it was supposed to work well together. Between crappy performance on some games and outright crashing on others I'm almost fed up with a GPU I sunk 1800 bucks on when I needed an upgrade in 2021. I wished I would have just went with NVIDIA and stayed with it. Despite its problems with games on occasion, I have had much more stability with NVIDIA than AMD ever was. Sadly I have to pay an extra 1400 bucks to resellers to get one. I learned my lesson the hard way.

I politely request you take a relook at this GPU.  I have the 6900 XT paired with a 5950X and there are several core issues that need to be addressed.  First and foremost, DX11 games are miserable with this GPU.  To the tone that my old GTX 1080 often outperforms the 6900 XT in such APIs.  In other cases, DX11 games are just unplayable.  Games like SC2 even now have a disclaimer stating that if you use an AMD GPU you must turn off shadows/lighting; even after taking such actions, the game will still inevitably crash, over and over.  Next, stuttering is a huge issue that must be addressed-- not just in gaming, but with watching Youtube videos or Twitch streams.  Perhaps the latter is the fault of another component (CPU or otherwise) but I can share the video stuttering is not due to internet bandwidth issues (direct fiber line) and I have done extensive testing to illustrate its associated strictly due to the components of the PC.  These stuttering woes (gaming and otherwise) go far beyond the known issue associated with TDP.  As I am most certainly not alone in my complaints, I hope you take the chance to review.  In fact, I am so far and beyond frustrated with this 5950X / 6900 XT combo that I will ship my PC to you for review.

I have a Gigabyte AORUS Master RTX 3090 right now. If I could get my hands on a 3080 to test out, I'd love to test out playability between the two cards within the VR space, because there's not really any benchmarks to speak of that are relevant to this use case.

text:
Its been a thing pretty much ever since auto-OC "boost" algorithms have been used.  Because modern cards will now use their boost algorithms to keep the card at the max clocks it can sustain while keeping its temperature target, if your card can maintain the same clocks at a lower voltage, the card will generate less heat, which will allow it to either boost higher if its stable, or keep its maximum boost clocks for a longer duration, which results in better performance.  Before boost algorithms, doing an "undervolt" would only lower the temps a little bit, and since most people who were modifying their clocks/voltages were doing so to overclock, you were already past the stock voltages anyways, so no one was testing how low they could set the voltages for stock clocks (they were doing the opposite, seeing how high they could get the clocks to run on the stock voltages, then raising both as high as they could or were comfortable with).  With the introduction of boosting algorithms and behaviors to CPUs and GPUs, it wasnt long before people figured out that an easy way to squeeze a little more performance out of a (basically) stock part was to lower the voltages as much as they could, which would get you some "free" performance without actually overclocking due to the boost algorithms behavior.

Its not just a GPU thing either.  Especially with AMDs PBO and now the introduction of the "Power Curve Optimizer", you can get some pretty healthy increases to performance by tweaking the voltages for your CPU.  Personally with my 5800X I was able to get Cinebench scores just a couple hundred points shy of a stock Threadripper 1950X by cranking the PBO as high as it would go and undervolting it with the Power Curve Optimizer (which is an incredibly handy and powerful tool if you use an AMD 5XXX CPU with PBO enabled, if you do, google some guides and such as its a great way to get a little more "free" performance).

text:
I can't bring myself to spend that kind of money on something that will usually be superseded in 12 months or so. I used to, but the last best of everything PC I built was way back in the days of Pentium 4 Extreme. That CPU costs me lots and was near worthless in a very short time. It hurt. I ordered the parts while I was at sea. I picked them up in port and went back to sea. Three months later when I got back to land the CPU was superseded by the much cheaper Core stuff (I think Phenom II as well, but I can't remember). 

I build mid range these days, but even mid range is reaching prices that are making me consider how fast that expenditure will be superseded. It is just how it is. A person has to be really into gaming to want to pay the prices. Now I am replacing parts every few generations or so instead. 

I probably will not rush out to play Cyberpunk. I'll wait a year or so until all the DLC and patches are included in a cheaper bundle. By then mid range cards will probably handle the GFX as well as higher range ones do today. I have other stuff I would rather spend money on like guitars etc (my PC is a digital audio workstation first and gaming machine second). Once you get a few miles on the clock, a year does not seem so long to wait (time seems to goes much faster once you get past about 29). 

I am the same about cars these days too. I had a RS Legacy Subi and then a S-type Jaguar. Really pricey cars. Waste of money. Next car will be a cheap used Toyota i think (import to NZ. Cheap as).

As for AMD vs Nvidia and Intel. I support AMD these days. I want to back the underdog, because I was concerned about tech monopoly and therefore monopoly prices. AMD are even earning that support these days. It has been a while since that happened. text: It's odd that this and Ryzen both show the same behavior where undervolting or increasing clocks silently kills performance for the sake of stability when really it should crash.  Has anyone done a deep dive on why this happens?
author: @alistairblaire6001

text:
Its a function of the "auto-OC" features that have been pretty much standardized in HW now with both CPUs and GPUs.  Even when you are manually overclocking parts now days (except for doing an ACTUAL manual OC on CPUs by locking the multiplier and voltages), you are still working within the auto-OC functionality (and even then you are still partially using the clock/voltage auto algorithms as clocks speeds have not been static for a very long time, so there is always SOME kind of auto tuning of clocks/voltages going on unless you manually disable every kind of p-state and other power saving feature, but even then Im pretty sure SOME power-saving down clocking behavior is unable to be disabled).  There are merits to both arguments whether its better to just have a "manual" OC actually BE a hard manual OC, where if you make a change that results in instability, you get crashes and/or undesirable effects (like artifacting, etc) as opposed to current functionality, where it is much harder to make changes that result in crashing, but consequently its much easier to put the card into a position where the systems in control of modifying voltage/clocks/etc end up in positions where performance suffers.

We are kind of at a weird in-between point where except for hardcore OCing (like liquid nitrogen), the benefits of OCs on standard ambient type cooling are diminishing rapidly as auto-OC boosting performance is rapidly approaching what you can get with a manual OC for both CPUs and GPUs (memory tuning is a little farther behind, but with XMP even that is starting to get redundant as well, especially with how low the performance gains are for OCing RAM in most situations).  Its likely that fairly soon the performance of boosting algorithms will make any OCing besides exotic cooling completely irrelevant.
